newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal rejects austere IMF budget remedy.
newsitem.headline: Portugal rejects austere IMF budget remedy.

text.p: Portugal on Tuesday rejected as "inappropriate" an International Monetary Fund call to impose a wage freeze and public service layoffs to meet economic targets for joining a single European Union currency.
"They (the IMF recommendations) are completely inadequate for the Portuguese situation," Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco said in a radio interview.
Speaking from Washington, where he is attending the IMF annual meeting, Sousa Franco said that the recommendations were "classic remedies taken from (economic) manuals".
"But we are going to act in accordance with Portuguese reality and not in accordance the manuals," he said.

Sousa Franco is drawing up the government's 1997 budget plan for cutting the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), one of the key requirements for joining the European Union's planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The deficit is estimated to be around four percent in 1996.
The government has said it can achieve its 1997 target and still give public service employees wage increases slightly above inflation, without cutting jobs or raising taxes.
The IMF also recommended a rise in Value Added Tax (VAT).
"It is not necessary to fire public sector workers or raise VAT to achieve our budget objectives," Sousa Franco said.
Earlier, the newspaper Diario Economico quoted the IMF as saying that Portugal could meet the 1997 deficit goal but only if it took tough action.
The Fund recommended a freeze on public sector wages, a reduction in the number of public sector employees and cuts in current spending by ministries.
"Our projections indicate that the mere freezing in nominal terms...will not be enough," the IMF was quoted as saying.

The government's rejection of the advice was generally supported by independent analysts polled by Reuters who said that Portugal should manage to achieve the necessary budget reductions without massive sacrifices.
Analysts said that the strengthening of economic growth, improved tax collection and moderate 1997 public sector wage increases should make it possible to achieve the deficit goal.

"If the economy grows at rates above 2.5 percent and if there is greater efficiency in the tax system and moderate public sector wage increases, it will be possible," said Isabel Cabral, economist with Lisbon broker Fincor.
